title: Spotting being agile and doing agile
blurb: Recognize when a team is only doing agile (events, tools, terms) and say what being agile would look like instead.
question: Larkspur's app team holds every Scrum event, but a monthly committee picks its stories and it may not change them. Is the team being agile or only doing agile?

teach.body: Formally: being agile means thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset to your work within appropriate levels of self-management. Doing agile is the practical application of agile frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology. In plain English: doing agile is what you can see (sprints, stand-ups, boards, new words); being agile is how people think, and whether they are free to act on it.

teach.h: Being vs doing at a glance
The two contrasts the exam uses (2.3.1)
head: Contrast
Being agile
Doing agile alone
teach.caption: If a stem shows rigid rule-following, think routine. If gains appear and then fade, think short-term mechanics.

root.label: Are agile events, tools or terms in use?

children.edge: Yes, but no freedom to decide or adapt
children.label: Doing without being

children.edge: Yes, and people adapt within limits
children.label: Being and doing

children.edge: No, but people think in an agile way
children.label: Being, little structure

items: Stand-ups run as status reports to a manager rather than a team plan for the day.
Retrospectives produce actions the team is not allowed to make.
Plans are renamed 'sprints' or a 'release map' but every task is still assigned from above.
The team follows the sprint backlog even when feedback shows it is wrong, without asking why.
Leaders call the project 'agile' while every small change needs their sign-off.

teach.body: If agile thinking is not instilled and people are not given appropriate freedom, calling processes, frameworks or techniques 'agile' is meaningless: the organization cannot actually be agile. This gap is what the book calls being versus doing agile. The fix is not to drop the frameworks, but to explain the why and let people act within agreed limits.

Larkspur Rail's app team has used Scrum for two years, with Owen Thackeray facilitating its events. Suppose finance director Dominic Faraday insists that a monthly committee approves every story and that stand-ups report to project manager Rhys Pengelly. That is doing agile. Being agile would see the team and its product owner adjust stories after passenger-panel feedback, within release tolerances, and use retrospectives to change how they work.

teach.text: Classic traps: doing agile is not wrong, it is just not enough on its own. Being agile does not mean unlimited freedom; it is acting within appropriate levels of self-management. Renaming things (sprints, release map) is still doing agile, and do not confuse this pair with the Agile Onion layers.

items: Being agile: thinking in an agile way AND being allowed to act on it within appropriate self-management (2.3.1).
Doing agile: applying frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology.
Adaptability vs routine; long-term impact vs short-term mechanics.
Calling something agile is meaningless if people cannot act in an agile way (2.3).

summary: You can now tell from a scenario whether a team is being agile or only doing agile, using the definitions and the two contrasts in 2.3.1. You can also choose the action that moves a team from rituals to a real mindset with freedom to act.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's app team holds every Scrum event on schedule. However, the stories for each sprint are chosen by a monthly committee chaired by the finance director, and the team may not change them, even after the passenger panel reports problems. Which statement BEST describes the team?
options: It is being agile, because it holds every Scrum event on schedule
It is being agile without doing agile, as the committee sets priorities
It is doing agile without being agile, as it cannot act on an agile mindset
It is applying neither, as Scrum events are not used in PRINCE2 Agile
A.why: Doing agile is applying frameworks and events; being agile also needs people to be allowed to apply an agile mindset within appropriate self-management (2.3.1). The team has the events but no freedom to act on feedback.

whyNot.0: Holding events is doing agile; it does not show the mindset or the freedom to act.
whyNot.1: The team clearly is doing agile (it runs Scrum); what it lacks is being agile.
whyNot.3: PRINCE2 Agile works with agile frameworks such as Scrum; teams may use their events.

A.q: After a Fair Fares sprint review, passenger-panel members say the one-tap claim screen confuses people with season tickets. Within the release's agreed tolerances, the product owner and the app team agree to rework the screen in the next sprint without waiting for a committee. What does this BEST show?
options: Being agile: acting on an agile mindset within agreed self-management
Doing agile: following the sprint review routine that Scrum requires
Doing agile: adopting Scrum terminology for the claim screen work
Being agile: deciding freely with no limits set by the governance
A.why: Being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset within appropriate levels of self-management (2.3.1); the team adapts to feedback inside agreed tolerances.

whyNot.1: Holding the review is doing agile, but the key point is the team acting on what it learned.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the stem is about terminology; it is about adapting to feedback.
whyNot.3: Being agile is within appropriate levels of self-management, not without limits.

A.q: Larkspur's customer relations team adopts a Kanban board and daily stand-ups. In the first month, claims are cleared faster. By month three the board is out of date, stand-ups have stopped and old habits are back. Which contrast from the book BEST explains this?
options: Adaptability versus routine in the team's work
Long-term impact versus short-term mechanics
Responsiveness and innovation from feedback loops
Vision versus adaptability from Table 2.3
A.why: Doing agile alone focuses on mechanics and may bring short-term efficiency gains that lack sustainable impact; being agile creates a cultural shift and long-term resilience (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: That contrast is about rigidly following a framework without the why; here the gains faded.
whyNot.2: Responsiveness and innovation is one benefit of agile (2.4), not a being-versus-doing contrast.
whyNot.3: Vision and adaptability are Table 2.3 qualities, not a being-versus-doing contrast.

B.q: Midway through a sprint, Larkspur learns that the train-running data feed will change format next month. The Coinbridge Payments team keeps building to the old format because 'the sprint backlog is locked', and nobody asks what the change means for passengers. Which contrast from the book does this BEST illustrate?
options: Long-term impact versus short-term mechanics
Customer collaboration versus contract negotiation
Empowerment versus respect
Adaptability versus routine
B.why: Doing agile alone may limit teams to following frameworks rigidly without understanding the why; being agile lets them adapt and think critically (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: That contrast is about gains that fade over time, not rigid rule-following now.
whyNot.1: This is an Agile Manifesto value, not a being-versus-doing contrast.
whyNot.2: Empowerment and respect are both mindset characteristics, not a 2.3.1 contrast.

B.q: Rhys Pengelly, Larkspur's project manager, now calls work packages 'sprints' and the stage plan a 'release map', and the board calls him the 'agile lead'. He still assigns every task to individual developers each morning. Which description is BEST?
options: Being agile, because agile terms are now used throughout
Agile terms are adopted, but people are not free to self-manage
Being agile, because the release map replaces the stage plan
Neither, because terminology is not part of doing agile
B.why: Adopting agile terminology is part of doing agile (2.3.1); without freedom to self-manage, the label is meaningless (2.3).

whyNot.0: New terms are doing agile; they do not show the mindset or freedom of being agile.
whyNot.2: Using a release map is an artifact choice, which is doing agile, not proof of being agile.
whyNot.3: Adopting agile terminology is part of the definition of doing agile.

B.q: Larkspur's app team holds stand-ups that are status reports to the project manager, and its retrospectives produce actions the team is not allowed to make. Which action is MOST LIKELY to move the team from doing agile towards being agile?
options: Let the team decide and make its own improvements within agreed limits
Add a second daily stand-up so the manager hears status more often
Introduce a new tool so that each person's tasks are tracked closely
Rename the retrospective a lessons workshop to match PRINCE2 terms
B.why: Being agile needs people to be allowed to apply an agile mindset within appropriate self-management (2.3.1); letting the team act on its retrospectives does that.

whyNot.1: More status reporting adds mechanics and control, not freedom to act.
whyNot.2: A new tool is more doing agile; it does not change how people are allowed to work.
whyNot.3: Renaming an event changes terminology, which is still doing agile.

C.q: Dominic Faraday, Larkspur's finance director, proposes telling the government that Fair Fares is 'fully agile' because the app team uses Scrum. Every change to a story, however small, still needs his personal sign-off. Is this an appropriate description of the project, and why?
options: Yes, because the app team applies a recognized agile framework
Yes, because every change to scope must be approved by the board
No, because the label means little if people cannot act in an agile way
No, because the finance director is not a member of the project board
C.why: If appropriate freedom is not allowed, labelling processes or frameworks as agile is meaningless; this is the gap between being and doing agile (2.3).

whyNot.0: Applying Scrum is doing agile; it does not make the project agile if no one may act on the mindset.
whyNot.1: Detail changes inside the project backlog are handled informally at team level; only baseline changes go formal.
whyNot.3: In the scenario, the finance director does sit on the project board.

C.q: In a retrospective, Larkspur's app team finds its estimates are poor and decides to try a different estimating technique next sprint. Project manager Rhys Pengelly insists that the project board must approve the change first. Is this an appropriate response, and why?
options: Yes, because the board approves the management approaches for the project
Yes, because managing by stages means the board controls each sprint
No, because retrospectives are run and owned by the project manager
No, because the team should be allowed to adapt within agreed self-management
C.why: Being agile means the team is allowed to apply its mindset within appropriate levels of self-management (2.3.1); a team-level change to how it estimates needs no board decision.

whyNot.0: The executive approves management approaches, but an estimating tweak inside a team is not a change to them.
whyNot.1: The board authorizes one stage at a time and delegates day-to-day control; it does not control each sprint.
whyNot.2: Retrospectives belong to the team; this option gives a wrong reason.

C.q: Passenger-panel testing shows the pre-filled claim confuses users with split tickets. The product owner and the app team swap a planned Could-have story for a fix of similar effort in the next sprint, without changing the project backlog. Is this an appropriate example of being agile, and why?
options: Yes, because the team adapts to feedback within its agreed self-management
Yes, because Scrum requires the sprint backlog to change after each review
No, because every change to a story must go to the change authority
No, because adapting mid-release breaks the zero tolerance on time
C.why: The team thinks in an agile way and is allowed to act on it within agreed limits (2.3.1). A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change handled at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.1: Scrum does not require a change after every review; the reason is acting on feedback within limits.
whyNot.2: Only changes that affect the project backlog go to the board or change authority; this is a detail change.
whyNot.3: Swapping work of similar effort keeps the sprint and release timeboxes, so time is not exceeded.

reteach.title: What you see vs how people think
reteach.question: Can you tell rituals from a real agile mindset?

blocks.body: Ask two questions. Are agile events, tools or terms in use? That is doing agile. Are people thinking in an agile way and allowed to act on it within agreed limits? That is being agile. A team can do every ceremony and still not be agile.

blocks.text: New labels (sprints, release map, agile lead) are still doing agile. Being agile is freedom within appropriate self-management, not freedom without limits.

explain.body: Being agile: thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset within appropriate self-management. Doing agile: applying agile frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology.

test.q: Larkspur's data team says it now 'does agile' because it uses user stories, a sprint board and two-week sprints. Which part of being agile does this statement leave out?
options: Applying a recognized agile framework to its work
Following agile processes and techniques each sprint
Using agile terminology in its team meetings
Thinking agile and being allowed to act on it
test.why: Being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset within appropriate self-management (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Applying a framework is part of doing agile, which the team already claims.
whyNot.1: Processes and techniques are part of doing agile.
whyNot.2: Terminology is part of doing agile.

explain.body: Adaptability vs routine: being agile adapts and thinks critically; doing agile alone may follow a framework rigidly without the why. Long-term vs short-term: being agile brings cultural shift and resilience; doing agile alone may bring short-term efficiency that does not last.

test.q: Larkspur's IT department has used Scrum for two years. Its teams follow each event exactly, but when a sprint goal turns out to be wrong they finish it anyway 'because that is the process'. Which contrast does this show?
options: Long-term impact versus short-term mechanics
Adaptability versus routine
Individuals versus processes and tools
Understanding versus vision
test.why: Doing agile alone may limit teams to following frameworks rigidly without understanding the why (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: That contrast is about short-term gains fading, not rigid rule-following.
whyNot.2: This is part of an Agile Manifesto value, not a 2.3.1 contrast.
whyNot.3: These are Table 2.3 qualities, not a being-versus-doing contrast.

explain.body: Look for events with no freedom: stand-ups as status reports, retrospectives with no power to change, new names for old plans, and leaders who call it agile while signing off every small change.

test.q: Which observation at Larkspur is the clearest sign of doing agile WITHOUT being agile?
options: The app team changes its stand-up time after a retrospective
The PO reorders stories after passenger-panel feedback
The stand-up is a status report to the project manager
The team swaps a Could-have story for one of equal effort
test.why: A stand-up run as a status report keeps the event but removes the team's self-management, which is doing without being (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: The team acting on its own retrospective shows freedom to adapt.
whyNot.1: Adapting priorities to user feedback is being agile.
whyNot.3: Trading stories of equal effort is the team adapting within its limits.

explain.body: Keep the useful structure, explain the why behind each practice, give people freedom to decide within agreed tolerances, and let feedback change the plan. Labels alone change nothing.

test.q: Larkspur wants its customer relations staff to be agile, not just to hold stand-ups. Which step would help MOST?
options: Explain the purpose of the change and let staff adapt their own work within agreed limits
Rename the existing weekly meeting a sprint review so the terms match the IT department
Buy a new digital board so that managers can track each person's claims in more detail
Add more stand-ups so the team leader can check progress twice a day instead of once
test.why: Being agile needs people to think in an agile way and be allowed to apply it within appropriate self-management (2.3.1); explaining the why and granting freedom builds that.

whyNot.1: Renaming meetings is terminology, which is doing agile.
whyNot.2: A tool for closer tracking adds control, not freedom.
whyNot.3: More check-ins are more mechanics and control.
